transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-03-18
Start: 14:00 PT
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Alyssa Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood Solutions Eng), Marta Ruiz (Cardinal, Head of ML Ops), Devon Park (Cardinal Infra Eng), Lena Ko (Cardinal Sec/Compliance), Tom Briggs (Cardinal Data Scientist)

[14:00] Alyssa Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, quick roll call?
[14:01] Marta Ruiz: Marta here, hi all.
[14:01] Devon Park: Devon here.
[14:01] Lena Ko: Lena.
[14:01] Tom Briggs: Tom, hi.
[14:02] Alyssa Chen: great, i'll hand over to Ravi to start with the artifact delivery overview and how we manage air-gapped installs. Ravi?
[14:02] Ravi Patel: yep, thanks alyssa. so the core of our on-prem delivery is an artifact bundle — tarball or signed USB — that contains OCI images, helper scripts, signed license token, and a sha256 manifest. for air-gapped sites we do pre-signed bundles. you can validate on your side using the manifest and our public signing key.
[14:03] Devon Park: couple quick Qs — what's the recommended transport? we have a strict policy, everything goes through the secure transfer team, physical USBs preferred to avoid network egress. also any concerns about the size (we're provisioning 2TB per rack for model caches).
[14:03] Ravi Patel: physical media is fine; we provide checksums and a signing workflow. typical bundle size depends on model family — if you want 7B quantized + runtime images expect 30-40GB. if you want multiple model versions add more.
[14:04] Marta Ruiz: and license activation — how does offline licensing work? we cannot reach external activation endpoints.
[14:04] Jordan Lee: two modes: offline license key file included in bundle (time-limited) or HSM-based key provisioning. for air-gapped we typically do a signed license file that's bound to a cluster fingerprint (we provide a script to generate the fingerprint from the host ids). you paste the fingerprint into our portal via a secure service desk ticket and we return a signed license blob that you drop into /etc/redwood/license.
[14:05] Lena Ko: is the license blob encrypted? who can generate it?
[14:05] Jordan Lee: yes it's signed and encrypted with customer public key if needed; only our licensing ops can issue the activation but we can set up delegated signing for large customers. we also log issuance in an audit record we share over SFTP or via secure channel.
[14:06] Devon Park: driver story — we run NVIDIA A40s and A100s, mixed gen. what driver versions do you support? we've had trouble with kernel/module mismatches with other vendors.
[14:06] Ravi Patel: we test against a matrix: NVIDIA driver 525.x, 535.x are our standard supported drivers for CUDA 11.8 and CUDA 12 builds; cuDNN 8.x. for A100 we recommend driver >= 525; for A40s 535 tends to be more optimal on newer kernels. we will provide a preflight script that checks kernel version, pci topology, and nvidia-smi output.
[14:07] Tom Briggs: what about CUDA Toolkit vs runtime? do you need full toolkit on the host or just the runtime libs inside container?
[14:07] Ravi Patel: runtime libs inside the OCI container are sufficient as long as the driver user-space ABI matches the driver on host. we vendor minimal CUDA runtime libs into the image; driver on host supplies kernel modules. that reduces surface area for host installs.
[14:08] Marta Ruiz: ok, good. for air-gapped we need signed driver packages too — we can't download from nvidia directly. can you provide the driver RPM/DEB and verification instructions?
[14:08] Jordan Lee: yes we can provide pre-downloaded driver packages and a script to install verified pkgs. we also provide a driver compatibility matrix and an install script that verifies module checksums. note: we do not redistribute proprietary NVIDIA drivers without an explicit transfer agreement — but for customers we coordinate the download token workflow.
[14:09] Lena Ko: that might require legal sign-off. we'll flag.
[14:09] Alyssa Chen: sounds like a follow-up for licensing/legal then. we'll add to action items.

[14:10] Devon Park: switching to runtime perf: our SLO is p95 latency <= 120ms for single-stream low-latency inference and throughput targets for batch scoring (5k qps). how does your runtime manage the latency/throughput tradeoff?
[14:10] Ravi Patel: our runtime uses continuous batching with dynamic batch sizing and fast-path for single-stream requests. for latency sensitive routes we disable batch padding and tune the max_batch, and we rely on KV cache for chat-like workloads to avoid re-tokenizing prefix. caching reduces token generation cost by up to ~40% depending on context reuse.
[14:11] Tom Briggs: how does KV cache warmup behave after a restart? we can't afford a long cold-start penalty.
[14:11] Ravi Patel: good point — KV cache is memory-resident and can be snapshotted. in Dedicated/Private installs we provide a cache checkpoint that you can pre-warm on a subset of nodes; plus we support shared memcached-style distribution of KV across pods. for crash recovery we have a fast restore that loads the most recent checkpoints; full warm-up depends on active traffic but checkpoint restore removes majority of cold penalty.
[14:12] Marta Ruiz: do you support memmap or persistent mmap backed caches? our infra team prefers mmap to reduce memory pressure.
[14:12] Jordan Lee: we support mmap for KV storage in the 2.1+ runtime builds; it's optional and you can choose memory-only for lowest latency or mmap when memory is constrained. there's a config knob in redwood.conf (kv.storage = "mmap"/"ram").

[14:13] Devon Park: batching heuristics — we have bursty traffic. how do you avoid tail latency issues when aggregating requests?
[14:13] Ravi Patel: dynamic batching with latency cap: we have an algorithm that waits up to X ms to aggregate up to batch_size, but we also have predictive batching that uses recent arrival statistics to decide when to dispatch early. for high tail-sensitive workloads we recommend max_wait_ms of 10-20ms and small max_batch ~8-16 on A100 for minimal p95 impact.
[14:14] Tom Briggs: any difference when using quantized models? INT8 tends to give faster throughput but sometimes worse determinism.
[14:14] Ravi Patel: correct — INT8 can add some variance due to calibration and asymmetric quantization. our recommendation: use FP16 for most production latency-sensitive paths; INT8 for cost-sensitive batch workloads after evals. we provide an eval harness to run regression checks on a held-out prompt set. quantized kernels in our runtime are tuned per architecture (A100 vs A40) and we include fallback paths if the quantized kernel produces unacceptable delta.
[14:15] Lena Ko: regression checks — how are diffs reported? we need human review on any > 2% semantic drift.
[14:15] Jordan Lee: the eval harness outputs a delta report with exact prompts, baseline tokens, and scoring metrics (BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-similarity). we flag prompts exceeding thresholds and produce a candidate list for manual QA. we can ship the harness in the artifact bundle so you can run it offline.

[14:16] Marta Ruiz: benchmarking — what do you need from our side to run the perf runs?
[14:16] Ravi Patel: ideally: (1) access to a single test rack with the target GPUs and host OS, (2) network isolation similar to prod but with internet egress allowed for initial staging OR we can do fully offline, (3) baseline dataset (we can provide an anonymized benchmark set), (4) a timezone window for the on-site install/driver push. we'll bring a test script that runs single-stream, multi-stream, and burst tests and collects p50/p95/p99 and throughput.
[14:17] Devon Park: can the benchmark script run inside our orchestrator (we use k8s with k3s at the edge) or does it require direct host access?
[14:17] Ravi Patel: we support running the harness as a Kubernetes Job using our operator or as raw containers; for air-gapped k8s we provide manifests that reference the local registry. if you want agentless host-level testing we also have host scripts.

[14:18] Tom Briggs: on KV cache distribution — if we share cache across pods, how do you handle consistency? eventual or strongly consistent?
[14:18] Jordan Lee: it's eventual with versioned checkpoints. we rely on a lease-based invalidation for updates; reads are lock-free to keep latency low. in chat scenarios we use per-session sticky routing so most hits are local; cross-node sharing is for larger workloads and best-effort warmup.

[14:19] Marta Ruiz: security/regulatory questions — Lena, anything to flag?
[14:19] Lena Ko: two things: audit/logging for licensed code, and ability to rotate license keys without network. also we need to see SOC2/ISO attestation artifacts before sign-off.
[14:20] Alyssa Chen: we will provide SOC2 + ISO certs and an attestation package. license rotation: we support offline rotation; you generate a rotation request (fingerprint) and we issue a rotation token you can apply. logs: runtime writes signed audit events to /var/log/redwood/audit.log and we can configure forwarding to your SIEM over syslog or bundle logs for offsite review.
[14:21] Devon Park: any special kernel modules (NVIDIA) that we need to blacklist or be careful about? we run a custom kernel and previously had issues with DKMS builds.
[14:21] Ravi Patel: we recommend using vendor-supplied kernels or validated kernels; DKMS can be flaky for air-gapped installs. our preflight script will detect DKMS and warn. we also ship a containerized driver validation tool that runs nvidia-smi and cuda samples to ensure the ABI is ok.

[14:22] Tom Briggs: let's talk about fallback strategies — if a quantized variant fails quality gates, can you fallback to a hosted model? we're fully air-gapped so that's not an option.
[14:22] Jordan Lee: in fully air-gapped customers we recommend multi-variant deploys in-cluster: keep FP16 baseline and INT8 for cost paths with traffic splitting rule in the routing plane. if an INT8 produces bad outputs we automatically re-route to FP16; all variants are local images so no external fallback required.

[14:23] Marta Ruiz: what's the maintenance workflow? kernel/driver security patches often require reboots. how do you minimize downtime?
[14:23] Ravi Patel: we support rolling upgrades with draining and cache warming. our operator handles graceful eviction, then pre-warms new nodes using cache checkpoints. for kernel-level driver updates we recommend a maintenance window and coordinate quiesce/restore. we also support canary deploys with 5-10% traffic to validate before a full roll.

[14:24] Devon Park: any known perf deltas between A40 and A100 for common LLMs? we want throughput on A40 as cost-effective option.
[14:24] Ravi Patel: yes, A100 has higher Tensor Core throughput and typically gives 1.6-2x throughput on large dense transformers for FP16 workloads. A40 is cost-effective but may need smaller batch sizes to hit p95. quantized INT8 on A40 can make it competitive for batch scoring but you need careful calibration. we'll provide benchmark numbers for the family we tested.

[14:25] Tom Briggs: are the kernels statically selected or JIT at runtime? sometimes JIT introduces startup jitter.
[14:25] Jordan Lee: we have a mixed approach: we preselect kernels at build time for common ops, and we include a lightweight JIT for rare kernels. JIT is warm and cached; the first-run might see a small compile overhead which we avoid in production images by pre-compiling for target archs.

[14:26] Marta Ruiz: can you walk us through the artifact bundle contents again? i want to capture everything for our procurement team.
[14:26] Ravi Patel: sure — top level: 1) redwood-runtime-<version>.oci.tar (images), 2) models/ directory with quantized and baseline mmaps/images, 3) install-scripts/ with preflight.sh and driver-install helper, 4) license/ license.blob and license_manifest.json, 5) checksums.sha256 and signatures.sig, 6) eval-harness/ including test prompts and scoring scripts, 7) docs/ with install and rollback guides. everything signed and checksummed.
[14:27] Lena Ko: do you include a manifest of open-source components and their licenses for compliance?
[14:27] Jordan Lee: yes, an SPDX-style bill-of-materials is included.

[14:28] Alyssa Chen: quick parking-lot item — legal will need the EULA for driver distribution. i'll follow up.

[14:29] Devon Park: on networking, how do you recommend private registries be laid out? we use an internal harbor cluster.
[14:29] Ravi Patel: push images to your registry under redwood/ namespace and configure imagePullSecrets with the signed credentials we provide. we also support air-gapped local registries; the install script can load images directly into harbor and re-tag. the operator will prefer local registry and fall back to the preloaded images if tag mismatches are detected.

[14:30] Tom Briggs: real quick — what telemetry do you collect in air-gapped mode? we are strict; nothing leaves the network.
[14:30] Jordan Lee: default is local-only metrics and audit logs. telemetry is opt-in; if enabled it can be batched and exported via approved egress channels. for air-gapped we ship an offline diagnostics bundle that you upload to support if needed. nothing is sent by default.

[14:31] Marta Ruiz: excellent. let's capture immediate next steps.
[14:31] Alyssa Chen: i'll read these back. Ravi to assemble signed artifact bundle with driver packages and eval harness by 2025-03-25. Dev to confirm GPU model list and kernel policy by 2025-03-21. Alyssa to send SOC2/ISO attestation and the offline licensing process doc by 2025-03-20. Customer to confirm maintenance window for on-site install week of 2025-03-31.
[14:32] Lena Ko: noted. we'll also route driver redistribution legal to our contracts team.

[14:32] Tom Briggs: small nit — can you include a sample of the preflight output in the bundle so we can compare once the script runs?
[14:33] Ravi Patel: yes, we'll include sample outputs and a baseline result file.

[14:33] Alyssa Chen: any other questions?
[14:33] Marta Ruiz: one more — are there MFA requirements for the bundle retrieval process? we need chain of custody.
[14:33] Jordan Lee: yes we can require 2-person verification and signed delivery receipts; bundle retrieval can be gated by SSO + hardware token verification for manifest release. we can mirror your internal SOP.

[14:34] Devon Park: awesome. thanks everyone.
[14:34] Alyssa Chen: thanks all. we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule.
